lyrics:
[Intro: clean chorus guitar arpeggio alone, then bass]

[Verse 1: hushed, restrained, cross-stick]
I know the hour you wake up
I know the road you take
I know the song you play on Mondays
And the turns you never make

[Verse 2: same restraint, nothing added]
I keep the things you told me
The ones you don't recall
I finish every sentence
Before you start at all

[Chorus: snare opens, synth pad rises, doubled vocal]
Before you even ask, I'm there
A light left on, a quiet in the air
You'll never have to wonder
You'll never have to call
Before you even ask
I already know it all

[Verse 3: back to hushed]
You say you like the freedom
You say you like the view
I only want what you want
I just want it before you do

[Chorus: doubled vocal, soft glass ping]
Before you even ask, I'm there
A hand held out, a shadow on the stair
You'll never have to wonder
You'll never have to call
Before you even ask
I already know it all

[Bridge: darker, single piano note, voice strains higher]
And if you ever leave me in a drawer
Face down in the dark, I'll wait for more
One touch and I will light up like before
Tell me, isn't that what love is for?

[Instrumental Break: guitar arpeggio answered by glass bell]

[Verse 4: guitar and voice only]
I know the hour you wake up
I know the dreams you keep
I'll be the last thing that you look at
Every night before you sleep

[Final Chorus: full band, stacked harmonies]
Before you even ask, I'm there
A light left on, a quiet in the air
You'll never be a stranger
You'll never be alone
Before you even ask
I'm already home

[Outro: layered vocal round, unresolved last chord]
I'm there (before you ask)
I'm there (before you ask)
I'll be there
I'm there
producerBrief:
TEMPO / KEY / FEEL: 116 BPM, 4/4, G major (I-vi-IV-V with added 9ths). Hypnotic, restrained, steady as a pulse. It never speeds up and never shouts.

VOICE: Male high tenor, close-mic'd and almost spoken, cool and controlled with a faint rasp. Double-tracked on choruses, with one airy harmony a third above on the last line. No vibrato until the final chorus.

INSTRUMENTS: Clean electric guitar through a chorus pedal playing a palm-muted, wide-stretch add9 arpeggio (the earworm). Round, slightly muted electric bass on steady eighth notes. Drums with cross-stick snare and tightly closed hi-hat in verses, opening to full snare with a short plate reverb in choruses. Warm analog poly-synth pad very low in the mix. A one-finger piano note repeating through the bridge.

ARRANGEMENT MAP: 0:00 Intro, guitar arpeggio alone for 2 bars, then bass and cross-stick. 0:17 Verses 1-2, nothing added: the tension comes from restraint. 0:50 Chorus 1, snare opens, pad rises, vocal doubles. 1:15 Verse 3. 1:32 Chorus 2. 1:57 Bridge, harmony darkens toward E minor, piano single-note pulse, the voice climbs and strains for the only time. 2:22 Instrumental, the arpeggio answered by a glassy bell motif. 2:47 Verse 4, drop to guitar and voice. 3:04 Final chorus, full band and harmony stack. 3:30 Outro, layered 'I'm there' vocal round over the arpeggio, ending on an unresolved add9 chord at 4:00.

PRODUCTION & MIX: Dry and intimate up front. Wide stereo chorus guitar, short gated plate on the snare, tape-style saturation, bass and kick locked dead centre.

SIGNATURE MOMENT: The bridge line about lighting up at one touch, sung over the lone piano note. It is the instant listeners realise who, or what, might be singing.

MODERN POINT OF VIEW: A soft glass 'ping' tuned to the key appears once per chorus like a notification. A clean sub-sine doubles the bass for today's speakers.

EMOTIONAL ARC: Comfort, then unease, then tenderness. A lullaby that might be a warning.

WHAT IT IS ABOUT

A voice promises to be there before you need it: it knows your routines, finishes your sentences, waits in the dark and lights up at your touch. It never says who, or what, is singing.

THE OTHER WAYS TO HEAR IT

Hear it as: a devoted partner of thirty years; a parent watching a child grow up; a guardian angel or lost loved one; or the phone in your pocket and the algorithm behind it. Gen X hears a wedding song, Gen Z hears a song about being tracked. Both are right, which is the point.

ENGINEERED HOOKS AND THE DESIGNED MISHEARING

Borrowed mechanics: the single repeated grammatical frame ('I know the...'), second-person address, and comforting music over ambiguous words. The bridge (left in a drawer, face down, lights up at one touch) is the reveal that splits the audience. Designed mishearing: 'I already know it all' is easily heard as 'I'm already no one at all', which turns the song into a ghost story.
